strengths: Achieves equivariance without computational overhead: Unlike existing equivariant networks, Platonic Transformers maintain standard Transformer efficiency while incorporating geometric constraints—a genuine practical advantage

Sound theoretical framework: Rigorous group-theoretic foundation with formal proofs of end-to-end equivariance (Proposition 1) and novel connection between RoPE and dynamic convolution (Proposition 2)
Comprehensive experimental validation: Diverse benchmarks across vision (CIFAR-10), 3D (ScanObjectNN, QM9), and molecular (OMol25) domains with systematic ablations on symmetry group choices
Principled weight-sharing scheme: Equivariance is achieved through constrained linear layers (Eq. 8) rather than adding complex modules, keeping the architecture elegant and maintainable
Theoretical novelty in attention analysis: Proposition 2 revealing RoPE attention as dynamic convolution with explicit Fourier series representation provides new understanding of attention mechanisms
Practical implementation details: Efficient Cayley table approach for group operations and Fourier domain implementation exploration (Appendix M) demonstrate engineering maturity
weaknesses: Instability with learned keys inadequately analyzed: The paper reports that mixed kernels (learned keys) were 'highly unstable' on QM9/OMol25 but only provides qualitative hypothesis without learning curves, gradient statistics, or rigorous ablations of alternative regularization schemes

Limited novelty: Core contribution is combining existing techniques (RoPE from Su et al. 2024 + group convolutions from Cohen & Welling 2016) rather than introducing fundamentally new equivariance mechanisms

Equivariance broken in practice: CIFAR-10 and ScanObjectNN experiments use APE and external reference frames that violate strict end-to-end equivariance, undermining claims about equivariance benefits on these tasks
Modest empirical improvements on non-equivariant tasks: CIFAR-10 +1.24%, ScanObjectNN +0.8% with discrete symmetry assumptions—insufficient to demonstrate value when true symmetry is absent
Discrete approximation quality not characterized: Using 12/24/60 rotations instead of continuous SO(3) is pragmatic but expressiveness loss is not quantified or analyzed

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds reported; most results appear to be single runs. QM9 results show suspicious precision (0.010 exactly matching EquiformerV2)

Missing analysis of when equivariance helps: No probing studies to verify learned models actually respect equivariances; no investigation of failure modes when true symmetry doesn't match chosen group; no analysis of learned representations

OMol25 results under short training: Only 22 epochs (Appendix L.2) raises convergence questions; comparison under different computational budgets (120 vs. ~475 hrs) makes advantage assessment difficult

Limited theoretical comparison: Claims that equivariant attention (orientation-dependent) is 'more expressive' than invariant attention lack formal justification; no empirical direct comparison on same tasks

Incomplete presentation of method: Architecture breaks equivariance at final predictions through pooling (Appendix G); interaction between frame-dependent position projection and translation equivariance could be clearer

strengths: Sound theoretical framework with rigorous group-theoretic foundations and correct proofs (Proposition 1, Proposition 2)
Elegant connection between RoPE-based attention and dynamic group convolution with linear-time complexity interpretation
Maintains standard Transformer computational cost through principled weight-sharing, unlike prior complex equivariant networks
Comprehensive experimental details with extensive appendices, reproducibility statements, and hyperparameter documentation
Clear presentation with helpful visualizations and well-structured exposition
weaknesses: Critical design choice inadequately justified: constant key vectors (k_j=1) required for stability on molecular systems but only addressed with speculation and no systematic investigation of when/why instability occurs
Large performance gap between attention and linear convolution modes (3-4% degradation, Tables 1-2) contradicts practical utility of theoretical linear convolution interpretation

Limited empirical advantages: CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN show marginal 1-2% improvements on non-equivariant tasks; QM9 matches but doesn't exceed EquiformerV2 (0.010 MAE); OMol25 experiments underpowered with constrained 120-hour budget vs. literature 475 hours
Equivariance claims overstated: 'no additional cost' is misleading; discrete Platonic approximation vs. claimed continuous SE(3)/E(3) equivariance; title suggests generality not fully supported

Inconsistent experimental methodology: different hyperparameter strategies for different datasets (extensive sweep vs. sequential process), weak T(n) baseline, no ablation validating equivariant vs. invariant attention, use of both APE and RoPE on CIFAR-10 complicates equivariance analysis
Constant key constraint fundamentally limits model expressivity compared to standard attention with learned keys, yet this limitation is not explored or justified beyond one remark

Missing critical analyses: no error bars/significance testing, limited comparison to recent equivariant Transformers, no failure case discussion, incomplete OMol25 evaluation without full computational budget
Fourier domain implementation (Appendix M) presented as future work but suggests spatial domain is suboptimal formulation

strengths: Elegant solution maintaining standard Transformer efficiency while inducing approximate E(n) equivariance through reference frames and group convolutions—resolves fundamental scalability vs. equivariance trade-off

Rigorous mathematical framework with formal proofs for end-to-end equivariance, dynamic group convolution connection, and linear-time complexity; insightful theoretical reinterpretation of RoPE through group theory
Remarkable computational efficiency with zero overhead vs. standard Transformers (2.79-2.85ms) and 2-3 orders of magnitude faster than specialized equivariant methods (G-Hyena 44ms, TFN 590ms)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (vision, 3D point clouds, molecular properties) with careful methodology, fair baselines, extensive ablations, and excellent reproducibility documentation
No architectural changes required—weight-sharing imposed on existing parameters enables immediate practical adoption; flexibility for symmetry breaking via external frames
weaknesses: Discrete approximation of E(n) via Platonic solid groups insufficiently analyzed—paper claims E(n) equivariance but only guarantees it for 12/24/60 discrete rotations; impact on continuous symmetry problems (QM9, OMol25) not quantified

Empirical performance gains often modest: CIFAR-10 +1.24%, QM9 α-property matches EquiformerV2, OMol25 outperforms eSEN on energy only under constrained budget; for methods emphasizing geometric fundamentals, improvements should be more substantial

Constant-key design choice (k_j=1) for linear-time complexity lacks theoretical justification—empirical instability on QM9/OMol25 is noted but root cause unexplained, and different behavior across tasks deserves investigation

Linear-time variant incurs substantial performance degradation (CIFAR-10: -2.93%, ScanObjectNN: -0.7%) undermining O(N) complexity benefit; practitioners will use full attention, limiting practical value of convolution interpretation

Incomplete baseline comparisons—limited recent equivariant Transformer benchmarks (SE(3)-Transformers not evaluated), FAFormer only on QM9, no systematic ablation of finite group choices beyond Platonic solids

strengths: Elegant resolution of efficiency-equivariance trade-off: achieves SE(n) approximation equivariance in Transformers with zero additional computational cost through principled weight-sharing

Rigorous mathematical framework with formal equivariance proofs (Propositions 3.1, B.1) and group-theoretic justification; novel connection to dynamic group convolution (Prop 4.1) provides theoretical insight

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across five diverse domains (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, QM9, OMol25, ProteinMD) with extensive ablations, multiple seeds, error bars, and detailed hyperparameter documentation
True computational parity demonstrated through wall-clock timing (Table 11); parameter reduction via weight-sharing (factor of |G|) with practical linear-time convolutional variant
Thorough reproducibility: promised open-source, clear architectural specs (Table 12), detailed implementation (Appendices E-L), realistic equivariance error analysis (Table 13)
Honest treatment of limitations: acknowledges approximate (discrete) equivariance, uncharacterized extreme-scale performance, and stability trade-offs in design choices (Appendix M)
weaknesses: Empirical gains are modest despite theoretical elegance: QM9 generation validity improves only 1.3 points (97.09%→98.43%), and paper's explanation that 'Transformers learn equivariant tasks better unconstrained at scale' undermines core motivation for adding geometric constraints

Theoretical-practice gap on central claims: (1) Proposition 4.1 equivalence to dynamic convolution assumes no softmax, but actual model uses softmax, making the connection approximate with unclear practical value; (2) claimed SE(n) equivariance is actually discrete approximation (12/24/60 rotations), not true continuous equivariance

Insufficient guidance for practitioners: group selection appears to be trial-and-error (Table 7) with no principled framework; fixed vs. learned keys require different stabilization strategies (QK norm) varying by task; need to 'break symmetry' with APE on some datasets suggests method applicability is limited

Limited comparison to equivariant baselines: most comparisons against standard (non-equivariant) Transformers; for molecular tasks, comparing general-purpose Platonic Transformers to specialized Equiformer variants is unfair; missing comparison to large standard Transformers with SO(3) data augmentation

Scalability concerns: extreme-scale performance uncharacterized; Fourier domain implementation (Appendix O) shows throughput gains only at moderately higher hidden dimensions (Table 14), suggesting poor scaling; ImageNet-1K results (Appendix G) show only parity with 39.9M params, not superiority

Incomplete task analysis: when does equivariance help? ProteinMD shows modest gains (1.80 MSE vs 2.11), QM9 generation gap is small. No failure case analysis or principled framework for predicting when equivariance is beneficial. Regularization effect on non-equivariant tasks under-explored

Brittleness in optimization: learned keys destabilize QM9 training without additional QK normalization (Appendix M); softmax-discretization interactions not analyzed; lack of theoretical understanding of when equivariance helps vs. hurts

strengths: Sound mathematical framework with correct formalization of group equivariance and clear proofs
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains (vision, point clouds, molecules, proteins) with careful controls
Interesting connection between RoPE attention and dynamic group convolution providing theoretical insight
Principled design preserving standard Transformer computation graph while incorporating discrete symmetries
Extensive implementation details and hyperparameter documentation supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (feature lifting, group convolutions, multi-frame attention) without new principles
Significant gap between theory and practice: Proposition 4.1 requires constant keys and no softmax, but experiments use learned keys and softmax; learned keys are optimization-unstable (Appendix M)
Discrete approximation conflated with continuous equivariance: paper claims E(n) equivariance but only achieves discrete subgroups; non-zero equivariance errors in Table 13

Unconvincing experimental results: no SOTA on any benchmark; improvements marginal and within noise; speedup claims compare different architectures; ablation (Table N.2) doesn't isolate equivariance from information flow benefits
Overstated 'no additional cost' claim: FLOPs identical but runtime overhead non-negligible (2.8ms vs 2.01ms standard Transformer); implementation complexity substantial
Missing critical ablation: no comparison to standard Transformer with equivalent parameters; weak evidence that gains come from weight-sharing vs. capacity
Unclear design choices: lifting procedure ambiguous for different modalities; outputs often pooled/averaged breaking equivariance; practical implications unexplored
Weak evidence equivariance helps beyond parameter efficiency: ImageNet-1K results (Table 9) show gains from parameter reduction, not better inductive bias

strengths: Novel, principled approach to achieving roto-translation equivariance in Transformers through weight-sharing without modifying computation graph or computational cost
Rigorous theoretical grounding with formal proofs (Propositions 3.1, B.1, 4.1) deriving equivariance from group theory and establishing RoPE-convolution equivalence
Genuine computational efficiency preservation verified by timing experiments; parameter reduction by factor |G| without capacity loss
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (vision, chemistry, protein dynamics) with careful computational budget matching and multiple ablations
Consistent improvements across all tasks despite approximate (discrete) equivariance: CIFAR-10 +1.13pp with 83% fewer parameters, OMol25 Force MAE 13.11→11.15 with 2.6× throughput
Excellent reproducibility: open-source code promised, exhaustive hyperparameters (Table 12), detailed experimental protocols, appropriate impact statement
Insightful analysis of design trade-offs (fixed vs. learned keys) with rigorous ablations showing optimization sensitivity and task-dependent requirements
Rigorous molecule generation validation using PoseBusters with near-perfect structural consistency scores, going beyond standard validity metrics
weaknesses: Approximate equivariance to discrete subgroups of O(n) rather than full continuous E(3); equivariance errors ~0.006 post-training (Table 13) are small but systematic and could accumulate in deep networks

Task-dependent design choices requiring domain expertise: QM9 needs fixed keys while OMol25 needs learned keys with QK normalization; learned keys cause training divergence without stabilization (Appendix M)
No consistent state-of-the-art performance: QM9 results (α=0.043) below PΘNITA (0.038); modest molecule generation gain (DiP-Tetrahedron 98.43% vs DiP-{e} 97.09% validity)

Limited guidance on group selection for new domains; choice of Tetrahedral/Octahedral/Icosahedral relies on extensive ablations rather than principled heuristics; 2D/3D restriction unclear for generalization
Incomplete comparisons: OMol25 only vs eSEN-sm (missing Equiformer); no comparison with specialized molecular methods (NequIP, Allegro) at matched scales; all timing on specific GPUs
Scalability uncharacterized at extreme scale; Fourier domain optimization (Table 14) only beneficial at hidden_dim≥1728; unclear whether equivariance benefits persist as model/data scale increase

Substantial hyperparameter variation across tasks (rope_sigma 1.0-18.0, different use_key and freq_init strategies in Table 12) suggests framework requires task-specific tuning despite 'drop-in' positioning
Linear attention vs convolution trade-off not well motivated: 5.31pp gap on CIFAR-10 (Table 1) lacks guidance on when linear variant is preferable despite O(N) complexity
